clue.text: Not unusual to have most of the week off?

definitions.text: to have most of the week off?

blocks.note: first meaning: ordinary, everyday, humdrum

blocks.clueFragment: to have most of the week off?
blocks.note: second meaning, read cryptically: to put in a single shift of labour and rest for the other six days

explanation.walkthrough: Split as WORK A DAY, the word describes someone who labours on one day only, leaving most of the week free.
explanation.definitionFit: Workaday describes ordinary, commonplace things, the stuff of routine working life rather than anything special.

clue.text: Quietly covering for team member

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
a layer is a covering, as of paint or dust

explanation.surface: Someone quietly stands in to cover for an absent teammate.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is one of the people making up a sports side, so any individual squad participant.

clue.text: Almost two letters from Athens, or the lot

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the phrase is dropped

blocks.note: the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta, written together

explanation.surface: Someone brings back a couple of Greek letters, or perhaps the whole set, from a trip to Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: The word itself comes from the names of those same two Greek letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The alphabet is every letter together, so it is the complete set or whole lot of them.

clue.text: One stupidly repeating standard nonsense

blocks.note: par is the standard or norm, as in golf
rot is rubbish or nonsense talk

explanation.surface: Someone mindlessly parrots the usual nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A parrot mimics words without understanding, so the bird stands for any person mechanically echoing others.

clue.text: Overindulged, set off pistol

indicators.note: to set off is to trigger or detonate, so the word is blown apart and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pampered brat fires off a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoilt child has been pampered and given too much, so has been overindulged by parents.

clue.text: The crockery may be flying

blocks.note: surface reading: plates and cups hurled across the room in a domestic row
setter's reading: the piece of tableware that, with flying in front, becomes a supposed alien spacecraft

explanation.surface: A furious quarrel where the plates start getting thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: A flying saucer is a UFO, so this one item of crockery is the one that famously flies.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucer is a small dish placed under a cup, an everyday item of crockery.

clue.text: Every route announced each time

indicators.note: announced means spoken out, so the phrase counts by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: every route is all ways

explanation.surface: A traveller is told all the routes over and over.
explanation.definitionFit: Always means on every occasion, without exception, so on each separate time.

clue.text: Perhaps salt water in quantity beginning to surge forward

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: a sea is water in vast quantity
opening letter of surge
on means forward, as in moving on

explanation.surface: Salt water in huge quantity, like the tide surging forward.
explanation.walkthrough: Salt is a verb here: to salt food is one way to flavour it.
explanation.definitionFit: To season food is to add flavouring, and salting it is one example of that.

clue.text: Scavenger who smooths the sand?

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who searches the shore for things to collect or sell
second meaning, read literally: one who runs a comb over the seaside

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical split into BEACH plus COMBER, someone combing the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: A beachcomber picks over the shoreline for flotsam and objects of value, a kind of scavenger.

clue.text: Christmas dinner perhaps a complete failure

blocks.note: first meaning: the bird traditionally roasted for the festive meal
second meaning: a flop, as a film or show that bombs

explanation.surface: A festive meal that turns out an utter disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The roast bird is the classic festive centrepiece, and a flop of a film or play is slangily called one.

clue.text: Finally whistle the proper spiritual

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the next word

blocks.note: closing letter of whistle
taken as written
real means proper or genuine, as in a real meal

explanation.surface: A referee at last blows the final whistle on a proper match.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means heavenly or otherworldly, delicate and not of this material world, hence spiritual.

clue.text: Be very afraid of abandoning resistance? Exactly

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving something behind, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: to dread something is to fear it greatly
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether fearing a fight means giving up resistance, and is told yes, precisely.
explanation.walkthrough: The word works as an adverb meaning exactly, as in dead right or dead centre.
explanation.definitionFit: As an intensifying adverb it means precisely or absolutely, as in dead on time or dead ahead.

clue.text: Shock: seat is the lowest possible level

blocks.note: to rock is to shock or stun, as news rocks a nation
the seat is the part you sit on, the backside

explanation.surface: A shocking discovery that the chair sits at floor level.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitting rock bottom means reaching the very lowest point, below which nothing can fall.

clue.text: Small suggestion we hear for simultaneous publication

indicators.note: we hear says the words are judged by how they sound spoken together

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
an indication is a hint or suggestion

explanation.surface: A little hint is overheard about articles going out in several papers at once.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, S and INDICATION run together into the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Syndication is selling articles or programmes to many outlets so they appear in several places at the same time.

clue.text: The battle of the doorbells?

blocks.note: first meaning: a fierce, closely fought contest or row
second meaning: the two-tone chime a doorbell makes

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like the title of a comic war between doorbells; the hyphenated term is both a hard-fought contest and the bell's chime.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard-fought, evenly matched fight is called this in British slang, and it also imitates the sound of a chiming bell.

clue.text: Detour is confusing stranger

indicators.note: something confusing is jumbled and muddled, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A diversion baffles a visitor who does not know the area.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider is someone who does not belong to a group or place, a person unfamiliar to it.

clue.text: Wild dog is annoyingly evasive: vote for decapitation

indicators.note: decapitation removes the head, so the first letter of the word is cut off

blocks.note: coy describes someone irritatingly reluctant to give details
taken as written

explanation.surface: A slippery politician dodges questions while urging a vote for an execution.
explanation.definitionFit: The coyote is a wild North American member of the dog family, related to wolves and jackals.

clue.text: Enable relaxing – in whalebone?

indicators.note: relaxing means loosening up, so the letters slacken and shift into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A corset stiffened with whalebone is let out to allow some relaxation.
explanation.definitionFit: Baleen is the horny plate material in a whale's mouth, traditionally known as whalebone.

clue.text: How angry can a kangaroo be?

definitions.text: How angry can a kangaroo be?

blocks.clueFragment: How angry can a kangaroo be?
blocks.note: surface reading: a jokey question about the temper of an Australian animal
setter's reading: an idiom for furious that fits a bouncing animal literally

explanation.walkthrough: The everyday phrase for being furious contains a word for bouncing about, which is exactly how a kangaroo moves.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means extremely angry, fuming, as if jumping up and down with rage.

clue.text: In Labour, for example, I found equality

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other, so the single letter sits within the larger word

blocks.note: Labour is an example of a political party
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone joins the Labour Party and finds fairness there.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is the British left-of-centre political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Parity means being equal, especially equal status or pay, so it is a synonym for equality.

clue.text: Carefully describe date and time to take in major film

indicators.note: to take in means to hold within, so the outer letters wrap around the film

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for date
an epic is a grand, large-scale movie
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A critic sets out a date and time to see a blockbuster and review it carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict is to portray or represent in words or pictures, giving a detailed account.

clue.text: Contemptible type using two hands only occasionally

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: odd-position letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A lazy, despicable person who rarely uses both hands to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone this amphibian is an insult for a loathsome, repulsive person.

clue.text: Time for breakfast

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for a prison sentence, as in doing time
second meaning: a hot oat cereal eaten in the morning

explanation.surface: Someone announces that the morning meal is ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time for breakfast' reads as a single call to the table; split it, and the first word is jail time.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal cooked in milk is a breakfast dish, and in British slang doing it means serving a jail sentence.

clue.text: First-rate introduction to reading?

indicators.note: the introduction to a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: prime means top quality, the best
opening letter of reading

explanation.surface: A top-class first book for a child learning to read.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes a first-class elementary reading book, which is just what the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: A primer is a basic textbook for teaching children to read, an elementary introduction to a subject.

clue.text: Old nurse goes to stretch

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
to tend is to nurse or look after

explanation.surface: A retired nurse heads off to do some stretching exercises.
explanation.definitionFit: To extend something is to lengthen or draw it out, which is what stretching does.

clue.text: Conceal what is on one’s phone

blocks.note: first meaning: to hide or shield from view
second meaning: the display surface of a mobile

explanation.surface: Someone hides whatever is showing on their mobile.
explanation.definitionFit: To screen something is to shelter it from sight, and the glass display of a mobile is also so called.
